profile.name: Ayyalah (Al-Ayyala)
profile.tagline: A traditional Gulf performance art simulating battle, featuring rhythmic stick-work.
profile.insight: On November 26, 2010, in Fujairah, 285 participants from three different tribes gathered to perform the largest recorded Ayyalah, demonstrating the dance's role in tribal unity.
profile.profile: Ayyalah is a traditional performing art from the United Arab Emirates and Oman that simulates a battle scene through synchronized movement, drum music, and chanted poetry. Two rows of men face each other, wielding bamboo sticks, swords, or rifles, while women often participate by tossing their hair in a ritual known as naash. Recognized by UNESCO in 2014, the dance serves as a symbol of national identity, tribal solidarity, and historical victory. It is performed at weddings, official ceremonies, and national celebrations, bridging generations through the transmission of cultural values.
profile.profile_long: Ayyalah, also known as Al-Yawlah or Al-Razha, is a cornerstone of the cultural heritage of the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman. Historically rooted in Bedouin tribal traditions, the dance was originally performed to celebrate victory following tribal conflicts or successful pearl diving expeditions. Today, it functions as a vital expression of national identity, solidarity, and the values of defense and peace. The performance is characterized by its martial origins, where the movements of the dancers simulate a battlefield. The structure of the dance typically involves two rows of men, often numbering around twenty in each line, facing one another. These participants carry thin bamboo sticks, which symbolize spears or swords, though in some variations, performers may use dummy rifles or actual swords. The choreography is highly synchronized, with the men moving their heads and sticks in unison to the rhythm of the drums. In the United Arab Emirates, the performance is often augmented by the presence of girls wearing traditional dresses, who stand at the front of the rows and perform the 'naash'—a ritual where they toss their long hair from side to side. This act is said to symbolize the protection of women by the warriors. The musical accompaniment is essential to the Ayyalah, consisting of large and small drums, tambourines, brass cymbals, leather bagpipes, and flutes. The melody is noted for having seven tones in an irregular, repeating pattern, which guides the movements of the dancers. The chanted poetry, which varies depending on the occasion, glorifies nomadic life and tribal virtues. The dance is inclusive, involving performers from diverse backgrounds and age groups, with the role of the lead performer often being an inherited position responsible for training others. The Ayyalah is not a static tradition; it has evolved into various regional forms, such as the Al-Harbiyya, where the chant dictates the movement, and the Al-Wahabbiyya, found in the rural and coastal areas of Ras Al-Khaimah and Fujairah, which utilizes weapons and is performed to a slower drum rhythm without the participation of women. In Oman, the dancers arrange themselves in two rows facing each other, moving forward and swaying back and forth to simulate the head of a moving camel. The significance of the Ayyalah was solidified on the international stage in November 2014, when it was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage. This recognition has bolstered efforts to preserve the dance, ensuring that the skills, values, and knowledge associated with the performance are transferred from one generation to the next. Modern adaptations have also emerged, such as the Al Meydan reality series, which introduced a competitive format similar to televised talent shows, and the annual Shaikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Championship, which keeps the tradition relevant for younger generations while maintaining its core, historical structure.

sections.origins_and_history: The Ayyalah originated as a Bedouin war dance performed after tribal victories. It historically served as a ritual for tribal unity when groups were threatened by enemies. In 2014, it was recognized by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves two rows of men facing each other. Participants carry bamboo sticks, swords, or rifles. They move their heads and sticks synchronously with the drum rhythm while hopping from one foot to another. Women participate in the naash ritual, tossing their hair.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music features large and small drums, tambourines, brass cymbals, leather bagpipes, and flutes. The melody consists of seven tones in an irregular repeated pattern.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men wear the traditional white dishdasha. Women wear traditional dresses. The dance is performed in open spaces during weddings, national celebrations, and official state visits.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed for weddings, national holidays, state visits, and football matches. It signifies tribal solidarity, victory, and the protection of the community.
sections.notable_figures: The lead performer is typically an inherited role responsible for training other dancers.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include the Razfah, Al-Harbiyya, Al-Wahabbiyya, and the Ardah. Omani versions feature a specific swaying movement to simulate a camel's head.
sections.lineage: The dance descends from Bedouin tribal war traditions and pearl diving celebrations.

basic_steps: Stand in two parallel rows facing the opposite line.
Hold a bamboo stick in the right hand.
Synchronize head and stick movements with the drum beat.
Hop lightly from one foot to the other in time with the rhythm.
teaching.formation: Two rows of dancers facing each other.
teaching.level_notes: Beginner: Focus on rhythmic stick movement. Intermediate: Incorporate the hop and synchronized head movement.

music_profile.sound_description: A percussive, rhythmic soundscape driven by drums and cymbals, layered with melodic flute or bagpipe lines and communal chanting.

movement_profile.footwork: Hopping from one foot to another.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Holding sticks, swords, or rifles; moving them up and down synchronously.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Two rows of dancers facing each other.
